speakers.name: Josh MacAlister
speakers.role: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education

contributions.text: I should probably start with an apology for keeping the House so late on a Monday evening. I am grateful for the House’s time. I would also like to say how grateful I am to have the opportunity to bring this important Adjournment debate to the House. I pay tribute to my neighbouring Members of Parliament for their support since the announcement of the closure of Leweston school, particularly the hon. Member for North Dorset (Simon Hoare), whose hard work, support and knowledge have been invaluable throughout. I also express my gratitude to the Minister for the kind offer of a meeting in two weeks, alongside the hon. Member for North Dorset and the right hon. Member for Gainsborough (Sir Edward Leigh). I am angry—not just at the decisions that resulted in the closure of Leweston school, but at what happened after the school closed. I am angry at a group of people who demonstrated a complete lack of urgency when it came to protecting people and property, who failed to support staff, who attempted to take credit for work done by others, and who attempted to pass responsibility for their mistakes elsewhere. This is a group of people who took over a school that had served the community
contributions.name: Edward Morello

contributions.text: It is truly incredible that VAT on private schools can lead to closures and what may happen as a result. Similarly, in Northern Ireland, without warning, St Anne’s primary school was given only 35 minutes’ notice before the Department of Education publicly announced its closure. Does the hon. Member agree that there must be rapid and effective communication with staff, parents and pupils when closures are being considered? That would help to reduce the uncertainty and distress if school closures do occur—and, unfortunately, there will probably be more of them.
contributions.name: Jim Shannon

contributions.text: I thank the hon. Member for his intervention. I shall be listing some recommendations that I would like the Government to look at in order to prevent such circumstances from arising again, not least the introduction of a minimum notice period. I am not a lawyer or an accountant, and I am not alleging that every failure was deliberate or malicious or attempting to prejudge any investigation. Whether these failures arose from negligence, incompetence or something more serious, they cannot be ignored. What is clear is that 550 students were left with no school place at no notice, 54 staff were left unemployed, and parents were left tens of thousands and, in some cases, hundreds of thousands of pounds out of pocket. The necessary regulators and the police must look at the evidence and use their best judgment, but when wrongdoing is established, those responsible must be held to account.
contributions.name: Edward Morello

contributions.text: I thank my hon. Friend for giving way, and for the great speech that he is making. Does he agree with Robert from West Coker, who was head of engineering at Leweston, that it is unacceptable that staff have been let go with zero warning and zero consultation, and does he agree with me that the Department for Education must do all that it can to help staff, pupils and parents from Yeovil and beyond with the transition to new schools that are actually in their areas?
contributions.name: Adam Dance

contributions.text: My hon. Friend and neighbour is entirely right. While the local authorities have done everything possible to accommodate the students who have been displaced, the fact is that we are asking the state school sector to absorb an enormous number of students at very short notice. There will invariably be problems associated with that, and I hope that the Department for Education will provide assurances about how it plans to support local councils in their plight. The financial difficulties facing the school did not appear overnight. The company’s accounts described declining pupil numbers, substantial discounting of fees, rising operating costs, pressure on cash flow, regular financial updates, and a business dependent on further funding and investment to continue trading. It states that during 2026, before the summer holidays had even started, management information and cash-flow forecasts showed increased pressure on working capital and liquidity. The owners knew that the school needed a huge amount of capital to remain viable, but the parents did not. They continued to pay fees, deposits, money for school trips and, in some cases, substantial lump sums for future terms and academic
contributions.name: Edward Morello

contributions.text: After years of dedicated service as a music director at Leweston, Rachel, from Milborne Port, has suddenly been left jobless after its sudden closure. Her own children were at the school. They have been offered alternative places, but those are guaranteed only if Rachel secures another job. Does my hon. Friend agree that displaced teachers and their families who have lost fees that were paid up front should receive immediate financial support? Does he also agree that there should be an immediate investigation of the school’s financial dealings, especially given the recent change of ownership, and its management?
contributions.name: Sarah Dyke

contributions.text: My hon. Friend and neighbour is absolutely right. There is a litany of failings and of families who have been affected by this and who understandably want answers, both from Concept Education and from the Department for Education. I hope the Minister will take this opportunity to provide answers for them and for us. What I want to know, and what those families deserve to know, is what happened to that money. Was it kept for its intended purposes, or were funds transferred elsewhere within the wider group? Relevant authorities must look into whether the ownership arrangements provided the proper protection for the school and the people who depended on it. The impact on the students has been enormous. Many began the new half-term without a confirmed school place. Ofqual has confirmed that it cannot arrange transfers between examination boards, which leaves some pupils at risk of having to relearn substantial parts of their GCSE or A-level courses. For pupils with special educational needs and disabilities, the disruption is even more serious. contributions.name: Edward Morello

contributions.who: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education (Josh MacAlister)
contributions.text: I thank the hon. Member for West Dorset (Edward Morello) for raising this important issue, for securing the debate, for highlighting the issues around the closure of Leweston school and for touching on the Government’s decision to apply VAT to private school fees—although I appreciate the debate is focused primarily on the school in question. As a former teacher, I know the central role that schools play in their communities. When they close, the impact on pupils, their families, school staff and wider communities can be significant. However, private schools are independent institutions and decisions about ownership, financial sustainability and closures are all currently matters for their proprietors. Private schools, like many private organisations may face business pressures from demographic change, financial viability and operating costs, and, as schools, they are subject to changing parental demand and fluctuations in pupil numbers.
